title: Engine Start — Duty Cycle, Cooling Periods and Start Performance at High Airfield Elevation

issue.reason: Original issue of the engine start duty cycle and cooling period performance entry.

abstract: Performance entry giving the permitted number of consecutive start attempts, the cooling period between them and how both change with airfield elevation and temperature.

sections.purpose: To give the flight crew the permitted start attempts, the cooling periods and the effect of airfield elevation and temperature on start performance.
sections.description: Each start attempt heats the starter, and the limit on consecutive attempts exists to keep the starter within its temperature capability rather than to protect the engine. Three consecutive attempts are permitted, followed by a cooling period of thirty minutes. A revised starter standard with a larger duty cycle is expected in service; when it arrives the figures for it will be given here, and until an aircraft is confirmed to carry it on both engines the figures below are the ones that apply. An aborted start counts as an attempt, and this is the point crews most often get wrong: a hot start abort followed by a cooling period and a second attempt has used two of the three permitted cycles before the aircraft has moved. At high airfield elevation and high temperature the available air mass is lower, the light-up is slower and an abort is more likely, which is exactly where the attempt count matters most.
sections.crew_procedure: Before the first start of the day at a high or hot airfield, brief the permitted attempts and the cooling period. Count every attempt, including an abort. If the permitted attempts are used, do not begin another; apply the cooling period in full. If the second engine cannot be started within the permitted attempts, return to the stand rather than attempting a cross-bleed start on a hot starter.
sections.limitation_note: Three consecutive start attempts, then a thirty minute cooling period. An aborted attempt counts as an attempt.

type_data.crew_action: Confirm the starter standard, count every attempt including aborts, and apply the cooling period in full.

title: Engine Start — Duty Cycle, Cooling Periods and Start Performance at High Airfield Elevation

issue.reason: Entry brought into the present tense for the revised starter standard now in service, with the both-engines rule and the aborted-attempt rule confirmed unchanged.

abstract: Performance entry giving the permitted number of consecutive start attempts, the cooling periods between them and how both change with airfield elevation and temperature and with the starter standard fitted.

sections.purpose: To give the flight crew the permitted start attempts, the cooling periods and the effect of airfield elevation and temperature on start performance.
sections.description: Each start attempt heats the starter, and the limit on consecutive attempts exists to keep the starter within its temperature capability rather than to protect the engine. Two starter standards are in service. With the earlier standard three consecutive attempts are permitted, followed by a cooling period of thirty minutes; with the later standard five are permitted with a fifteen minute cooling period. The later figures may only be used when both engines carry the later starter, because the crew has no way of telling which starter is fitted to which side in the moment and a mixed aircraft must be treated as being at the earlier standard. An aborted start counts as an attempt, and this is the point crews most often get wrong: a hot start abort followed by a cooling period and a second attempt has used two of the three permitted cycles before the aircraft has moved. At high airfield elevation and high temperature the available air mass is lower, the light-up is slower and an abort is more likely, which is exactly where the attempt count matters most.
sections.crew_procedure: Before the first start of the day at a high or hot airfield, confirm from the technical file which starter standard the aircraft carries and brief the permitted attempts and cooling period. Count every attempt, including an abort. If the permitted attempts are used, do not begin another; apply the cooling period in full. If the second engine cannot be started within the permitted attempts, return to the stand rather than attempting a cross-bleed start on a hot starter.
sections.limitation_note: With the earlier starter standard: three consecutive start attempts, then a thirty minute cooling period. With the later standard fitted to both engines: five consecutive attempts, then a fifteen minute cooling period. An aircraft with one engine at each standard is limited to the earlier figures. An aborted attempt counts as an attempt. The both-engines rule and the aborted-attempt rule were both written before the later standard entered service and were re-examined against it at its release; neither needed changing and both are carried forward unaltered, which is recorded here so that the question is not re-opened at the next revision.
